facts.statement: The genus Stangerochampsa was first described in 1996 by Wu and colleagues.
facts.quote: Stangerochampsa was described in 1996 by Wu and colleagues.

facts.statement: The genus name honors the Stanger family, who owned the ranch where the specimen was found, while the species name honors James Ross McCabe, the discoverer and preparer of the fossil.
facts.quote: The generic name honors the Stanger family, the owners of the ranch where the specimen was found, and the species name honors James Ross McCabe, who discovered, collected, and prepared it.

facts.statement: Stangerochampsa is described as small to medium-sized, with a type skull measuring 20.0 cm in length and 13.0 cm in width, and a thigh bone 14.2 cm long.
facts.quote: Stangerochampsa is described as "small to medium–sized"; the type skull is 20.0 cm long from the tip of the snout to the occipital condyle, and is 13.0 cm wide at its greatest, while the thigh bone is 14.2 cm long.

facts.statement: Stangerochampsa possessed heterodont dentition featuring large crushing teeth located at the rear of its jaws.
facts.quote: It had heterodont dentition, with large crushing teeth at the rear of the jaws.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Stangerochampsa was discovered in the late Campanian to early Maastrichtian-age Horseshoe Canyon Formation in Alberta.
facts.quote: It is based on RTMP.86.61.1, a skull, partial lower jaws, and partial postcranial skeleton discovered in the late Campanian–early Maastrichtian-age Horseshoe Canyon Formation.

facts.statement: Brochu (1999) suggested that Stangerochampsa and Albertochampsa were synonymous and placed the genus just outside the family Alligatoridae.
facts.quote: Brochu (1999), in an analysis of all alligatoroids, found Stangerochampsa and Brachychampsa to be just outside Alligatoridae, and suggested that Stangerochampsa and Albertochampsa were synonymous.

facts.statement: Brochu (2004) and Hill and Lucas (2006) found Stangerochampsa outside of Alligatorinae, with Hill and Lucas identifying Albertochampsa as its sister taxon.
facts.quote: Brochu (2004) and Hill and Lucas (2006) also found Stangerochampsa to be outside of Alligatorinae; Hill and Lucas found Albertochampsa to its sister taxon.

facts.statement: Recent studies have yielded conflicting placements, with Stangerochampsa recovered as a stem-group caiman in 2021 and as a basal alligatorine in 2022.
facts.quote: Stangerochampsa was recovered as a stem-group caiman in 2021, but it was also recovered as a basal alligatorine in 2022.

facts.statement: Stangerochampsa is classified within the unranked family Globidonta.
Stangerochampsa lived during the Maastrichtian stage, approximately 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Maastrichtian to Maastrichtian (72.2 to 66 million years ago)

rejected.statement: Wu and colleagues classified Stangerochampsa as part of a clade within Alligatorinae, placing it closest to Brachychampsa, followed by Albertochampsa and Hylaeochampsa.
rejected.quote: Wu and colleagues, using phylogenetic analyses, found their new genus to be closest to Brachychampsa, and then Albertochampsa and Hylaeochampsa successively, as part of a clade within Alligatorinae.

rejected.quote: On the other hand, in the phylogenetic analysis conducted by Bona et al. (2018) Stangerochampsa was recovered as an alligatorid, specifically as a stem-caiman.
